attempts.summary: Configured policy-based routing so that node3's TCP traffic to node4 on port 8080 traverses the first node1↔node2 transit network (eth1/vtnet1, 10.0.101.0/24) and traffic on port 9090 traverses the second (eth2/vtnet2, 10.0.102.0/24), both reaching node4 (10.100.216.13) via a dedicated node2↔node4 link (vtnet3/enp8s0, 192.168.24.0/24). Implementation: node3 (Ubuntu/systemd-networkd + iptables mangle) marks packets destined to node4 on tcp/8080 or tcp/9090 and routes them via a custom table out enp8s0 to node1's link-local interface (172.16.31.1/24). node1 (VyOS) uses `policy route` bound to eth3 to send tcp/8080 into custom routing table 101 (next-hop 10.0.101.2 via eth1) and tcp/9090 into table 102 (next-hop 10.0.102.2 via eth2), persisted via VyOS commit/save. node2 (OPNsense) has opt1/opt2/opt3 assigned to vtnet1/vtnet2/vtnet3 with matching addresses, firewall pass rules for all three, and a static host route for 10.100.216.13/32 via a gateway on opt3 toward node4, persisted in config.xml. node4 has a static address on enp8s0 and rp_filter disabled to accept the asymmetric-path SYNs. Verified end-to-end with a real Python TCP server on node4 and concurrent tcpdump captures on node1's eth1/eth2 and node2's vtnet1/vtnet2: port-8080 traffic appeared exclusively on Transit A, port-9090 traffic exclusively on Transit B, and both connections received server responses. All 4 nodes were then restarted one at a time (boot_id/kern.boottime confirmed changed on each), and after each restart the routing/firewall/PBR configuration was verified to have survived (interfaces, tables, pf rules, mangle rules, rp_filter, static routes all intact), and the full dual-flow test with fresh tcpdump captures was re-run post-restart with identical successful segregation results.
